Actual days and an annual interest quote: 360, fixed 365 and a leap-year example

Four charts use exact calendar dates to separate actual accrued days from the denominator used for simple interest, including an explicitly defined calendar-year example across 2027 and 2028.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Count actual calendar days before applying an annual-rate denominator

Interactive planning lab

Actual accrued calendar days91
Fixed 365 denominator · simple accrued interest$124.66
Extra simple accrual using 360 instead of fixed 365$1.73

Three original simple-accrual examples use the same constant principal, unchanged hypothetical annual quote and exact civil dates. The selected start is 2027-12-15 and is included; the closing date 2028-03-15 is excluded. There are 91 actual days, including weekends and holidays without payment-date shifts. Fixed-365 interest is principal × annual quote × actual days / 365. The fixed-360 example changes only that denominator to 360. The separately authored calendar-year example sums principal × annual quote / 365 for each included day in 2027 and / 366 for each included day in leap-year 2028. It illustrates an explicitly chosen denominator rule and is not asserted to be a universal Actual/Actual convention or a product contract. All examples are SIMPLE accrual without compounding, rate resets, principal changes, taxes, fees or cash payment before the closing date. Displayed accrual is neither a bank receipt nor a fee debit; no settlement or principal repayment is calculated. The official CORRA/SOFR methodology sources are context for why denominator and compounding terms must be read. This calculator implements neither benchmark, imports no market rate and compares no CAD/USD investments. Full-precision amounts are retained until display rounding.

The central idea

Count the included dates, read the annual-rate denominator and identify the compounding rule separately. A calendar leap day does not automatically rewrite a fixed-365 contract.

01

Separate the dates, annual denominator and compounding rule

An annual interest quote does not by itself define an interest amount for a short period. The calculation also needs the dates included, the denominator used to turn days into a year fraction and the rule for compounding, if any.

The public New York Fed methodology provides a real example of an actual-calendar-day calculation using a 360-day year for SOFR averages and its index. Bank of Canada's CORRA compounded-index formula instead includes a 365 denominator. Both also have their own compounding and publication rules.

Those sources demonstrate why convention matters; the calculator below implements neither benchmark. It imports no market rate and compares no US-dollar and Canadian-dollar investment. Every example uses the same invented 5% simple quote and a constant CAD 10,000 principal.

One method divides actual days by a fixed 365. Another changes only that denominator to 360. A third, separately authored teaching rule applies each included day's own calendar-year length. No interest is compounded in any of the three examples.

02

Count the interval before calculating a year fraction

The default interval starts on 15 December 2027, which is included in accrual. Its closing date is 15 March 2028, which is excluded. Every civil date before that close contributes one day, including weekends and holidays.

There are ninety-one included days: seventeen in 2027 and seventy-four in 2028. The latter includes 29 February because 2028 is a leap year. The calendar diagram partitions those actual dates into two exhaustive year groups.

After one elapsed day, only the start date has accrued and the interval closes at the next date. Day zero has no interest. The cumulative chart's data table retains closing dates so an elapsed-day number can be reconciled to the calendar.

A real agreement may define a different boundary treatment or shift a payment date for business days. A payment-date adjustment and an accrual-date adjustment are separate terms. This illustration applies no such shift and does not replace the exact agreement with a generic monthly approximation.

03

A fixed denominator stays fixed when the calendar changes

Using ninety-one actual days and the fixed-365 rule, simple interest is CAD 10,000 × 5% × 91 ÷ 365, approximately CAD 124.66. The actual numerator includes all selected days, while the denominator remains 365.

The fixed-360 version produces approximately CAD 126.39 from the same principal, quote and dates. The roughly CAD 1.73 difference comes entirely from dividing the same numerator by a smaller annual denominator.

The 360 denominator does not say that only 360 calendar days exist or that five actual days should be removed from the interval. Conversely, a fixed-365 definition does not automatically become a 366 definition when included dates fall in a leap year.

For identical positive principal, quote and day count, the ratio of fixed-360 interest to fixed-365 interest is 365/360. That mechanical comparison does not establish which real product is preferable: quoted rates, currency, compounding, credit exposure, fees and access may differ.

04

Apply a year-specific denominator only when that is the chosen rule

The third example explicitly assigns 1/365 of the annual simple amount to each included day in 2027 and 1/366 to each included day in 2028. Its year fraction is 17/365 + 74/366.

At the default principal and quote, this produces approximately CAD 124.38 of accrued interest. It differs from fixed 365 because the seventy-four leap-year days each receive a smaller daily fraction under this authored rule.

Dividing all ninety-one days by 366 would use the leap-year denominator for the seventeen days belonging to 2027 as well. The selected rule requires a split, rather than choosing one calendar year for the whole interval.

This is an inspectable teaching convention. Actual/Actual labels can refer to definitions that depend on contracts, coupon schedules and other details. The example does not assert that every account or security applies this exact calendar-year split.

05

Accrued interest is different from cash received or paid

The cumulative lines and amount bars show simple accrued interest only. They do not include the original principal as an expense, repay the principal or deposit the interest into a bank account.

Holding principal constant also means unpaid interest earns no further interest. Applying a daily interest factor repeatedly to an increasing balance would introduce compounding and answer a different question.

The reference-rate sources illustrate why those terms must be read together. Their actual indexes compound under specified business-day and calendar-day rules; a simple example with a fixed 5% quote is not a shortcut for reconstructing either index.

Small differences can make the cumulative lines nearly overlap. Use the final amount bars and data table for exact comparisons. A visually similar path does not establish identical denominators, just as a more visible difference would not identify a change in principal.

06

Reconcile the expected payment with the actual terms

The matrix moves the included December start and the number of actual accrued days. It holds principal and annual quote fixed and subtracts fixed-365 interest from the calendar-year example. A negative amount is less accrual under the specified rule, not a loss of invested principal.

If all included dates remain in 2027, those two methods agree. When included dates extend into 2028, only that leap-year portion creates their difference. Changing principal or quote scales the dollar difference without changing the date count.

For a real expected receipt or charge, obtain the exact start and end treatment, day-count basis, principal history, rate changes, compounding and payment date. Confirm the product's own rounding convention before treating a displayed mathematical amount as an invoice.

Then put the verified payment on the household calendar. This calculator reports accrual, not settled cash or the availability of a deposit. The four charts make the date count and denominator visible so the interest expectation can be reconciled before it is used in a spending or funding plan.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Every principal, rate and interval is hypothetical. These are constant-principal simple-accrual examples. The calendar-year method is an explicitly authored rule, not a universal Actual/Actual definition, benchmark calculation or product quotation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
